fullName: X-ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy beamline. Wide-angle XPCS at 8-ID-E and small-angle XPCS at 8-ID-I.

status2026.detail:
The APS directory lists 8-ID as operational and accepting general users in 2026. It was the first APS-U feature beamline to host users. The first post-upgrade APS user run began on 16 September 2024. The 8-ID page dates its general-user operation from October 2024, while news reports a University of Akron group as the first users in early November during final commissioning. These sources differ slightly on the start date.

The XSD Dynamics & Structure group operates 8-ID-E for wide-angle XPCS and 8-ID-I for small-angle XPCS and Rheo-SAXS-XPCS. The stations run one at a time. The earlier GISAXS/GIWAXS program moved from 8-ID-E to 9-ID-D, CSSI, leaving E dedicated to wide-angle XPCS. The ring first reached 200 mA on 4 February 2025.

Six workers emptied the old E/I enclosures in under 14 days, as reported on 3 October 2022. December 2023 installation slides show the SAXS detector positioner and WAXS goniometer on the experiment floor.

tagline: Motion of atoms and nanoparticles is measured from changes in coherent X-ray speckle patterns.
summary:
At 8-ID, researchers measure motion from changes in interference patterns called speckle. This method is called X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, or XPCS. Coherent X-rays maintain a consistent phase relationship. Their scattering pattern depends on the positions of particles or atoms and changes as those positions change. Researchers measure motion over small distances and short time intervals, including inside samples that are opaque to visible light.

Cameras record up to 56,000 frames per second, and software calculates correlations between frames. Two stations operate in turn. At 8-ID-E, researchers measure atomic-scale motion with wide-angle scattering. At 8-ID-I, they study larger structures with small-angle scattering and a detector up to 12 m away. In late 2024, 8-ID became the first upgraded feature beamline to host users.

whatAPSUEnables.text:
Faster motion requires shorter XPCS frames, leaving fewer photons per frame. The upgraded electron source is about 15 × 4 µm rms in design brightness mode, compared with 275 × 10 µm before. At a fixed energy, coherent flux scales with brightness. The design coherent flux gain at 20 keV is roughly 250 to 500-fold. This supports measurements of weak scatterers such as proteins and dilute particles. Coherent X-rays up to 25 keV also penetrate rheometers, furnaces and pressure cells.

When photon counts limit the measurement, minimum frame time scales inversely with coherent flux squared. A 100-fold gain gives 10,000-fold shorter frames at fixed acquisition time, contrast and pixel count. At fixed frame time, the signal-to-noise gain is 100-fold. Detector speed and dose limit these gains. They are design values; no published as-built coherent flux measurement was found by October 2026.
quantitative: For an undulator optimized for 20 keV, the predicted coherent flux is 312 × 10¹¹ ph/s in APS-U brightness mode and 148 × 10¹¹ in timing mode, compared with 0.6 × 10¹¹ for the 2019 APS. The design gain is about 250–500×.
The Rigaku 3-Mpixel detector provides 19.2 µs continuous frames and about 1 µs burst frames. The design time-resolution goal is 100 ns.
The design brightness at 20 keV is 325 × 10²⁰ ph/s/0.1%BW/mm²/mrad² in brightness mode, compared with 0.6 × 10²⁰ before the upgrade.

Before the upgrade, the electron source at the insertion device was 280 × 10 µm rms, horizontal × vertical. The nominal zero-current APS-U values are about 14.5 × 3.1 µm in flat-beam mode at κ = 0.1 and 12.3 × 8.3 µm in round-beam mode. The APS public summary rounds these to about 15 × 4 µm and 275 × 10 µm, with up to 500× higher brightness.
The measured APS-U horizontal emittance was 33 pm·rad at the full 200 mA in April 2025. At reduced current with full coupling, it was below 30 pm·rad.
For one transverse mode with Si(111) and κ = 0.1, the SA-XPCS design coherent flux is 1.7 × 10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV, 7.2 × 10¹² at 15 keV and 2.0 × 10¹² at 25 keV.

The PDR compares one 1 × 1 coherent mode at 0.01% bandwidth. It predicts 6 × 10¹² ph/s at 12 keV and 9 × 10¹¹ at 20 keV for APS-U. The respective values are 8 × 10¹⁰ and 2 × 10¹⁰ at PETRA III P10, and 8 × 10¹⁰ and 5 × 10⁹ at NSLS-II CHX.

Before the upgrade, 8-ID-I provided about 2 × 10¹⁰ ph/s at 7.4 keV through a 20 × 150 µm horizontal × vertical coherence-defining slit. It used a Ge(111) monochromator with about 0.03% bandpass and two 3.3 cm Undulator A devices. Measured speckle contrast was about 10%. Several horizontal modes were present, so this is a partially coherent beam benchmark rather than a strict one-mode value.

The directory lists 10¹³ ph/s at 9 keV with Si(111) and 3 × 10¹² ph/s at 9 keV with Si(311). It lists a focused beam of 6 × 3 µm and an unfocused beam of 20 × 20 µm. It does not specify whether these are coherent or total flux values.

Before the upgrade, the UFXC32k prototype at 8-ID-I reached 826 ns burst frames and 19.36 µs continuous frames in 2018. In 2021, the Rigaku XSPA-500k ran at 52 kHz with 20 µs frames, with up to about 10⁹ frames a day reduced in near real time.
The original 2015 APS-U proposal targeted dynamics from 10 ns to 1,000 s and length scales from 1 nm to 5 µm. This would expand the XPCS dynamic range by up to six orders of magnitude.
APS publications quote accessible time scales of 100 ns to 1,000 s for APS-U-era XPCS. For WA-XPCS, the stated range is "gapless coverage from µs to hours".
Expected raw data volume is up to about 20 PB a year, compared with about 0.1 PB a year at pre-upgrade 8-ID. A Rigaku 3M at 56 kHz produces about 164 GB/s of raw data.

The Gaussian-beam estimate here uses the Kim convention, zero current, 10 keV and a 4.7 m undulator. It gives a coherent fraction of about 9% for the APS-U flat beam and about 0.06% for the 2019 APS, a gain of about 160×. Energy spread is omitted.

The 2021 WA-XPCS instrument table lists 1–2 × 10¹² ph/s for one coherent mode with Si(111) over 8–25 keV. This is about 10× below the FDR/PDR one-mode values at 8.8–10 keV. The cause is not documented; possible explanations include KB/CRL losses, different assumptions or a typographical error.

The 2015 Early Science report describes about 10,000 coherent modes in the pre-upgrade APS beam near 11 keV and a coherent fraction of order 10% with APS-U. This is consistent with the estimate here of about 0.06% before the upgrade and about 9% after it.
The APS Strategic Plan 2025–29 states a "4-to-6-order-of-magnitude increase in the time resolution of XPCS" and accessible time scales of 100 ns to 1,000 s.

techniques.name: Small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy
techniques.text: Small-angle XPCS measures motion over distances from about a nanometre to a micrometre in nanoparticles, polymers and proteins. Scattering angle sets the scattering vector q; smaller angles correspond to larger structures. Software calculates the intensity autocorrelation g_{2} to measure how each speckle pattern changes with delay. For freely diffusing particles, decay time scales as 1/q². Jammed or glassy materials often have decay times proportional to 1/q and faster-than-exponential decay, consistent with internal stress relaxation. At 8-ID-I, the spot is 3 to 10 µm and the detector distance 4 to 12 m. A 12.4 keV experiment at 11.6 m covered q = 0.04 to 0.51 nm⁻¹.

techniques.name: Wide-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, including Bragg and diffuse XPCS
techniques.text: Wide-angle XPCS measures motion of atoms and crystal domains, including rearrangements in glasses and charge or magnetic fluctuations. A small focus produces larger speckles, so the 8-ID-E spot is 0.3 to 3 µm with detector distances of 1.5 to 4 m. At 10 keV, the long-distance positioner reaches q about 4.7 Å⁻¹. At wide angles, scattering from different sample depths and beam positions creates large path differences. Narrow energy bandwidth preserves contrast across those differences. The Si(311) setting has a longitudinal coherence length of about 4.6 µm at 10 keV, compared with 0.9 µm for Si(111). This length is the path difference over which interference remains coherent.

techniques.name: Rheo-XPCS, or Rheo-SAXS-XPCS
techniques.text: Rheo-XPCS combines mechanical measurements of a fluid under shear with speckle measurements of its nanoscale structure. The rheometer is offered with Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials. Fluid lies between concentric cylinders in a Couette cell. The beam crosses the velocity-gradient direction, so scattering resolves motion along the flow and cylinder axis. Stress, strain and recovery are measured alongside speckle. Two-time and heterodyne analyses distinguish mobile and arrested regions, including shear bands and jammed networks.

techniques.name: Pinhole ultra-small-angle scattering / US-XPCS
techniques.text: In pinhole ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering, or USAXS, the sample is at 8-ID-E and the detector at the far end of the 8-ID-I tube, about 22 m away. This distance separates small scattering angles across more pixels, providing access to structures up to micrometres across and their slow motion by US-XPCS. The 2021 functional requirements specify a 15 to 45 µm beam.

techniques.name: Two-time correlation and higher-order analysis
techniques.text: Two-time correlation compares every pair of detector frames rather than averaging over all times. The resulting map, C(t_{1}, t_{2}), has time on both axes. Distance from the diagonal corresponds to delay, and position along it to sample age. Changes in map width and shape identify slowing, aging or abrupt motion that time averaging would combine. At 8-ID, graphics processors compute maps in near real time using boost-corr, and pyXPCSviewer displays them. Machine learning assists classification. Higher-order and spatio-temporal analyses remain under development.

techniques.name: Heterodyne XPCS / X-ray velocimetry
techniques.text: Scattering from moving particles interferes with scattering from stationary particles. This heterodyne interference produces oscillations whose frequency depends on flow speed. In the correlation function, the term is cos(q·vτ), where v is velocity and q is the scattering vector. Only the velocity component along q is measured. Applications at 8-ID include flow, convection and shear-thickening networks. A newer transport-coefficient analysis estimates flow in systems far from equilibrium.

scienceCases.title: Shear thickening in dense suspensions
scienceCases.text: Dense suspensions resist flow more strongly above a shear-thickening threshold. At 8-ID-I, Rheo-XPCS measured silica particles of 200 and 360 nm in polyethylene glycol at 56 to 60.5% volume fraction during shear and for at least an hour afterward. Heterodyne oscillations indicated mobile particles moving relative to a jammed frictional network. Stress relaxed quickly, while structure and dynamics changed much more slowly. Publication timing suggests the data preceded the upgrade shutdown; the run date is not confirmed.

scienceCases.title: Recovery of soft glasses after shear
scienceCases.text: An 8-ID study measured nanoscale motion during recovery of a soft glass after 300% strain. Stress decayed almost logarithmically with the loss of recoverable strain, and a convection-like backflow separated regions moving differently. The experiment used 12.4 keV X-rays, an 8 × 8 µm spot and an EIGER2 X CdTe 4M detector at 11.6 m. The preprint gives no run date. The distance exceeds the old station maximum of about 10 m, suggesting post-upgrade measurements.

scienceCases.title: Intermittent atomic motion in a metallic glass
scienceCases.text: A zirconium-based metallic glass was measured at pre-upgrade 8-ID-E for 83 hours at 668 K, below its glass transition, with one frame every 2.5 s. These materials lack a periodic crystal structure. Steady aging alternated with abrupt cluster rearrangements, and motion approached anomalous diffusion rather than ordinary Fickian diffusion. The measurement used a 10 µm beam at 7.32 keV near the main diffraction halo, q about 2.6 Å⁻¹. The upgraded source and narrower-band Si(311) setting at higher energy support measurements of faster atomic motion.

scienceCases.title: Nanoparticle motion at liquid interfaces
scienceCases.text: Particles and molecules collect at liquid–liquid and liquid–solid boundaries in solvent extraction, drug delivery and flow batteries. Binding energies may be only a few times the thermal energy kT. Buried interfaces are often inaccessible to confocal light microscopy. The 2019 Final Design Report identifies these interfaces as a principal small-angle XPCS application. Small coherent beams at higher energies are needed to measure particle arrangement and motion through surrounding material.

scienceCases.title: Fluctuations in quantum materials
scienceCases.text: Charge-density waves and magnetic domains in quantum materials fluctuate over time. Wide-angle XPCS, including speckle near Bragg reflections, measures these fluctuations. The July 2023 first-experiments workshop included charge-density-wave fluctuations in TaS₂ and lattice dynamics in microelectronics. These are proposed research directions relevant to microelectronics and quantum computing, rather than published 8-ID results.

scienceCases.title: Diffusion and aggregation of biomolecules
scienceCases.text: Diffusion rates provide hydrodynamic sizes of viruses and proteins in solution. Changes in these sizes indicate aggregation. Before the upgrade, 8-ID-I measured Cowpea mosaic virus with 19.2 µs time resolution and found a hydrodynamic radius 43 to 104% larger than the particle radius, depending on buffer. The APS Strategic Plan for 2025 to 2029 targets early protein aggregation, including pairs of molecules, at upgraded 8-ID. Dose limits the measurements, so sample flow and higher energies are needed.

scienceCases.title: Flow in driven soft matter
scienceCases.text: A transport-coefficient analysis of two-time speckle correlations estimates nanoparticle motion in systems driven out of equilibrium. It was first checked against molecular-dynamics simulations. Applied to earlier 8-ID-I creep and recovery measurements of charged silica at 42% volume fraction, it resolved populations moving at different speeds. These included neighbouring shear bands that a time-averaged correlation would combine.

keyParameters.label: Energy range
keyParameters.value: 8–25 keV design; directory 6–25 keV, with continuously tunable 7–25 keV
keyParameters.note: The 2019 FDR and 2021 functional requirements give 8–25 keV. The 2021 talk lists 4.8–25 keV for WA-XPCS. The directory specification gives 6–25 keV, while its special-capabilities text states "continuously-tunable beam energy from 7 keV to 25 keV".

keyParameters.label: Monochromator bandwidth
keyParameters.note: The directory rounds the Si(111) and Si(311) bandwidths to 10⁻⁴ and 3 × 10⁻⁵. The 2021 talk quotes 0.005–0.014%, or 5 × 10⁻⁵ to 1.4 × 10⁻⁴, for monochromatic beam and 0.5% for pink beam. The PDR predicts about 100× the Si(111) flux with pink beam.

keyParameters.label: Directory flux
keyParameters.value: 10¹³ ph/s at 9 keV with Si(111); 3 × 10¹² ph/s at 9 keV with Si(311)
keyParameters.note: The directory lists a focused beam of 6 × 3 µm and an unfocused beam of 20 × 20 µm. It does not specify whether these are coherent or total-beam flux values.

keyParameters.label: Design coherent flux in one mode with Si(111)
keyParameters.value: 1.7 × 10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV; 7.2 × 10¹² at 15 keV; 2.0 × 10¹² at 25 keV
keyParameters.note: The SA-XPCS calculation uses κ = 0.1, two 3 mrad mirrors and Si(111). FDR Table 4.34 lists 1.6 × 10¹³ for WA and 1.7 × 10¹³ for SA at 8.8 keV in one mode, labelled ph/s/0.1%BW. The 2021 WA-XPCS table lists 1–2 × 10¹² ph/s for one mode with Si(111) over 8–25 keV, about 10× lower. The difference is unresolved.

keyParameters.label: Focal spot in 8-ID-E, wide-angle
keyParameters.note: CRL-1 and the KB pair provide zoom focusing. The FDR simulation at 14.2 keV gives FWHM spots from 0.22 × 0.21 to 4.1 × 5.1 µm².

keyParameters.label: Focal spot in 8-ID-I, small-angle
keyParameters.note: CRL-1 and CRL-2 provide zoom focusing. The FDR simulation at 14.2 keV gives spots from 3.0 × 2.0 to 11 × 8.5 µm². The USAXS mode uses 15–45 µm.

keyParameters.label: Sample–detector distance, 8-ID-I
keyParameters.value: 4–12 m, telescoping and rotatable through 5°
keyParameters.note: The 2021 specification gave 2–12 m. The FDR flight path extends from 68 to 79 m.

keyParameters.label: Sample–detector distance, 8-ID-E
keyParameters.value: 1.5–2 m on the diffractometer arm; 2.5–4 m on the long-distance detector positioner
keyParameters.note: The long-distance positioner covers 2θ = 3–55° horizontally. The PDR vertical arm range is −1 to 120°.

keyParameters.label: Pinhole USAXS distance
keyParameters.value: ≈22 m, from the sample in 8-ID-E to the detector in 8-ID-I

keyParameters.label: Fastest time resolution
keyParameters.value: 19.2 µs continuous; ~1 µs burst
keyParameters.note: The design goal is about 100 ns. For comparison, the APS-U 48-bunch spacing is 76.7 ns.

keyParameters.label: Detectors
keyParameters.value: Rigaku Si 3 MPix, 56 kHz and burst ≈1 MHz; Eiger CdTe 4 MPix, 4 kHz
keyParameters.note: The public Rigaku model name is unspecified. The 2024 computing strategy calls it "UHSS 3M" and plans 56 kHz with 3.0 MB frames, or 164 GB/s raw, and 8.5 kHz with 6.0 MB frames. The XSPA family uses the UFXC32k ASIC with 76 µm pixels, 56 kfps continuous 2-bit readout, bursts of 13 frames at 970 kfps and 48 ns minimum exposure. The 2026 arXiv paper names an EIGER2 X CdTe 4M. The directory lists 4 kHz for the Eiger, matching the computing-strategy plan of 4.0 MB frames at 4 kHz, or 1 byte/pixel, and 16 MB frames at 1 kHz. Reduced-bit-depth operation is inferred from these values rather than explicitly stated.

keyParameters.label: Undulators
keyParameters.value: 2 in-line revolver undulators, each with 2.1 cm arrays at N = 112 and 2.5 cm arrays at N = 94
keyParameters.note: At the 8.5 mm device minimum gap and zero emittance, E1 is 8.34 keV for U21 and 4.54 keV for U25. The user minimum gap is 9.0 mm. The table footnote gives an effective period count of N − 2 because of the end poles.

keyParameters.label: Front end
keyParameters.value: HHLFE, windowless, 2 × 2 mm² exit mask at 25.4 m; limits 21 kW, 590 kW/mrad²

keyParameters.label: HHL mirrors
keyParameters.value: 2 × flat Si, 3.0 mrad, Si/Cr/Rh/Pt stripes, ~16 mm horizontal offset

keyParameters.label: Storage ring
keyParameters.value: 6 GeV, 200 mA; 324 bunches at 11.4 ns or 48 bunches at 76.7 ns; 42 pm design and 33 pm measured at 200 mA
keyParameters.note: The ring first reached 200 mA on 4 February 2025. The emittance measurement is from the April 2025 APS-U update. Bunch spacings follow from the 3.681 µs revolution period.

keyParameters.label: 8-ID-E sample environments
keyParameters.value: 3.5–475 K cryostage; furnace to 1,100 °C; tensile stage from liquid-nitrogen temperature to 350 °C

keyParameters.label: 8-ID-I sample environments
keyParameters.value: Anton Paar MCR 702e Couette rheometer; 9-sample, 3-zone holder at 0–160 °C

keyParameters.label: Data volume
keyParameters.value: Up to ≈20 PB/yr raw, compared with ≈0.1 PB/yr before the upgrade

keyParameters.label: Beamline length
keyParameters.value: ≈81.6 m to the end of 8-ID-I; beam stop at 80.6 m
keyParameters.note: The hutch end was read from the 2021 drawing. The beam-stop position is from the FDR.

keyParameters.label: Controls and data analysis
keyParameters.value: Bluesky and caQtDM experiment control; NX client remote access; Python and GPU correlation analysis with boost-corr; pyXPCSviewer
keyParameters.note: The 2024 computing strategy reports completed multi-τ and two-time algorithms on CPU and single GPU. Higher-order and spatio-temporal correlations were still in development.

insertionDevices.name: Upstream revolver APS21R25 #10
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator, with two magnet arrays on a rotating support
insertionDevices.notes: APS21#15 has a 21 mm period, N = 112, Keff = 1.38 at 8.5 mm and E1 = 8.34 keV. APS25#12 has a 25 mm period, N = 94, Keff = 2.01 and E1 = 4.54 keV. Length is N × λu, about 2.35 m. The user minimum gap is 9.0 mm. The magnets are NdFeB with grain-boundary-diffused heavy rare earth and vanadium-permendur poles, as specified for APS-U HPMUs in FDR Chapter 3. The arrays are mounted at 90° on a common support. An interlock requires the gap to be open before rotation.

insertionDevices.name: Downstream revolver APS21R25 #4
insertionDevices.notes: APS21#9 has a 21 mm period, N = 112, Keff = 1.38 and E1 = 8.36 keV. APS25#7 has a 25 mm period, N = 94, Keff = 1.99 and E1 = 4.58 keV. The FDR specifies two in-line U21/U25 revolvers with 4.6 m total length and maximum power of 2.0/2.2 kW through the 2 × 2 mm² mask.

source.canting: There is no canting. Two in-line revolvers occupy one straight and provide a single beam. FDR Table 3.13 places a phase shifter and corrector between the devices.
source.frontEnd: The standard APS-U High Heat Load Front End is based on the 28-ID HHLFE. In order along the beam, it contains the clearing magnet, LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM1, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor IM1, safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, front-end valve, exit mask and exit collimator. The exit mask at 25.4 m has a 2 × 2 mm² aperture and XBPM2. The collimator at 26.1 m has a 5 × 5 mm² aperture. Power limits are 21 kW and 590 kW/mrad². Differential pumping provides a windowless exit to preserve coherence.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence:
The nominal zero-current storage-ring parameters give the electron beam at the insertion device. In flat mode at κ = 0.1, with horizontal/vertical emittances of 39.7/4.0 pm, σx = 14.5 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.1 µm and σy′ = 1.29 µrad. In round mode at κ = 1, the emittance is 28.7 pm per plane and the respective values are 12.3 µm, 2.34 µrad, 8.3 µm and 3.47 µrad.

FDR Table 1.1 includes intrabeam scattering at 200 mA. For 324-bunch brightness mode at 42 pm, the respective values are 14.7 µm, 2.8 µrad, 3.2 µm and 1.3 µrad. For 48-bunch timing mode at 32 pm, they are 12.9 µm, 2.5 µrad, 8.8 µm and 3.7 µrad. The pre-upgrade APS values are 280 µm, 11.6 µrad, 10 µm and 3.4 µrad.

Shi and colleagues measured the source by grating interferometry at 3-ID-B in 2025, at 11.3 keV and 50 mA. At low coupling, εx = 44 ± 3 pm and εy = 3.3 ± 2 pm, with a total photon source of 16.1 × 4.9 µm rms. At full coupling, the horizontal and vertical emittances were 28 ± 3 pm and 31 ± 2 pm. Horizontal emittance was measured as 33 pm rad at 200 mA in April 2025.

For a 4.7 m effective undulator at 10 keV, the single-electron photon terms estimated here with the Kim convention are σr ≈2.7 µm and σr′ ≈3.6 µrad. In flat mode, the total photon source is about 14.7 × 4.1 µm rms with divergence about 4.6 × 3.9 µrad rms. The transverse coherence length λ L/(2 π Σ) at CRL-1, 52 m from the source, is about 70 µm horizontally and 250 µm vertically at 10 keV.

branches.name: Common optics in 8-ID-A, transport and 8-ID-D
branches.description: Both stations share the undulators, front end, high-heat-load mirrors, HDCM, optional DMM, CRL-1 and diagnostics along one beam axis.

branches.name: Wide-angle XPCS at 8-ID-E
branches.description: CRL-1 and KB mirrors focus monochromatic beam to 0.3 to 3 µm at the six-circle diffractometer. Detectors are on the arm at 1.5 to 2 m or the LDDP at 2.5 to 4 m.

branches.name: Small-angle XPCS at 8-ID-I, beam-pass through E
branches.description: Pink or monochromatic beam passes through a removable pipe in E. CRL-1 and CRL-2 provide a 3 to 10 µm focus at I, with a 4 to 12 m flight tube. Pinhole USAXS uses the E sample position and I detector, about 22 m apart.

components.name: Upstream revolver undulator APS21R25 #10, U21/U25
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate and not specified by a source. Two roughly 2.35 m devices share a roughly 5 m straight with a phase shifter between them. The upstream centre is placed about 1.25 m before the straight centre, which is the FDR distance origin.
components.text: The alternating magnetic field in this 2.35 m undulator deflects 6 GeV electrons from side to side, producing a narrow X-ray beam. Two magnet rows with 21 mm and 25 mm periods sit at 90° on a rotating support. Period is the repeat length of the magnetic pattern. With the gap open, rotating the support selects the row with higher flux at the chosen energy. This arrangement is called a revolver. At the 8.5 mm minimum gap the lowest fundamental energy is 4.54 keV with the 25 mm row and 8.34 keV with the 21 mm row; users work at gaps of 9.0 mm or more.

specs.periods: 21 mm with N = 112; 25 mm with N = 94

components.name: Phase shifter and corrector between the revolvers
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate, between the devices at the straight centre. FDR Table 3.13 lists "phase shifter/corrector" for the 08-ID dual in-line configuration.
components.text: A small magnet delays electrons between the two undulators so radiation from the second reinforces radiation from the first. Steering correctors here keep the electron orbit straight. The design lists a phase shifter/corrector at this spot, but its type and exact position are not published.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator APS21R25 #4, U21/U25
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate. The upstream-device note explains the source-position basis.
components.text: A second identical revolver undulator is installed directly behind the first. With both set to the same magnet array and gap, and radiation kept in phase, the effective source length is 4.7 m. The combined brightness is higher than that of either device alone. Up to about 12 keV, experiments use the fundamental of either array. Above roughly 12–14 keV, the selected energy is the 25 mm array's third harmonic, three times its fundamental. The 21 mm array's fundamental reaches about 16 keV only at a large gap, where flux is low.

specs.periods: 21 mm with N = 112; 25 mm with N = 94
specs.harmonics used: fundamental to ~12 keV; U25 3rd harmonic above ~12–14 keV

components.name: High-heat-load front end, HHLFE, windowless
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the front end occupies roughly 14–25 m inside the tunnel and through the ratchet wall; 20 m is a representative position for the GRID-XBPM/photon-shutter group. Component positions are not tabulated in the FDR.
components.text: The front end controls and shields radiation between the accelerator and beamline, inside concrete shielding. Water-cooled masks trim the beam, X-ray beam-position monitors check that it points exactly right, and shutters block it completely. This standard high-heat-load design of the upgraded APS is rated for 21 kW in total and 590 kW/mrad² at the centre of the beam. Differential pumping separates the vacuums without an exit window, avoiding window-induced changes to coherence.

specs.XBPMs: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask

components.name: Front-end exit mask, 2 × 2 mm²
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The front-end exit mask has a 2 mm square opening. Seen from the source 25.4 m away, the opening spans only about 79 microradians. A microradian is a millionth of a radian. Only the central core of the undulator beam enters the beamline. A beam-position monitor, XBPM2, is built into the mask. The preliminary design had asked for an even narrower 40 × 40 µrad for this beamline.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator, 5 × 5 mm²
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The front-end collimator is a tungsten block with a 5 mm square opening. Bremsstrahlung is high-energy radiation emitted when stored electrons encounter residual gas in the ring. The collimator confines this radiation. For the upgrade the opening was narrowed to 5 × 5 mm² to contain bremsstrahlung even with small lateral shifts of the X-ray beam.

components.name: White-beam HHL slits, 8ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Four tungsten-edged jaws trim the white beam, which contains the full undulator spectrum. The opening, up to 5 × 5 mm², sets beam transmission and coherence. A narrower opening passes a weaker beam with higher coherence. The whole assembly sits on a motorized table, for scanning a fixed aperture across the beam without changing blade spacing.

components.name: Mirror M1, flat Si, horizontal deflection; 8ID-MR-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: X-rays strike a flat silicon mirror at a grazing angle of 3.0 mrad, or 0.17°, and reflect horizontally. The predicted absorbed power is about 370 to 425 W. Four stripes, bare silicon, chromium, rhodium and platinum, have different upper reflection energies. Stripe selection filters unwanted high-energy harmonics. Reflection is horizontal throughout the beam-conditioning optics before the experiment stations. The source is several times wider than it is tall, so horizontal angular vibration produces less relative source broadening. A side notch in the mirror cuts heat-induced bending about tenfold.

components.name: White/pink-beam diagnostics, 8ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Staff align the undulator beam on the mirrors using a camera and position monitor. The preliminary design pairs a white-beam position monitor with a fluorescent yttrium aluminium garnet screen, or YAG screen, that works even with the undulator gap nearly open, a photocurrent monitor and a bypass aperture.

components.name: White-beam stop / mask, 8ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Straight-through white beam and bremsstrahlung are absorbed by a block between the mirrors. Only the pink beam reflected by M1, which still spans a broad band of energies but has lost the highest ones, passes the stop to the second mirror.

components.name: Mirror M2, flat Si, horizontal deflection; 8ID-MR-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight. Listed in the FDR table as 'Horizontal, Focusing', whereas the FDR text describes both mirrors as flat with an optional bender on M2.
components.text: At the second silicon mirror, a 3.0 mrad reflection returns the beam parallel to its original path, with about 16 mm lateral displacement. It has the same four reflecting stripes as M1. M1 has already absorbed most of the power, so M2 absorbs only 10 to 18 W. The design allows a mechanical or thermal bender to correct wavefront distortions from M1 and the monochromator; whether one is fitted is not documented.

components.name: Secondary collimator, 8ID-SC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Stray radiation is confined to the first optics enclosure by a lead-and-tungsten shielding block. The collimators here work with those in the front end, so the sideways-shifted beam passes while straight-through radiation is stopped.

components.name: Pink-beam mask / stop, 8ID-PM-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The pink beam passes through a mask opening, and radiation outside it is absorbed. Pink beam is mirror-filtered but retains a broad energy band. The built-in stop blocks the pink beam when inserted.

components.name: Bremsstrahlung collimator, 8ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Primary bremsstrahlung is absorbed by this dense shielding block before it reaches experiment stations. All of this primary bremsstrahlung is stopped in the first optics enclosure, which is why the second optics enclosure needs no collimators of its own.

components.name: Pink-beam diagnostics, 8ID-BD-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Beam position is measured just before the monochromator crystals. Knowing where the beam lands on the crystals is the first step to keeping it steady downstream.

components.name: Pink-beam slits H+V, 8ID-SL-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The pink beam is trimmed before the crystal monochromator to reduce unwanted radiation and heat.

components.name: Horizontal crystal monochromator, HDCM, LN₂-cooled Si(111)/Si(311), 8ID-MN-1 and -MN-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: X-rays are reflected by two liquid-nitrogen-cooled silicon crystals when their wavelength matches the crystal spacing and angle under Bragg's law. This selects a narrow energy band. The Si(111) setting passes a band about 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ of the energy wide; Si(311) passes one about five times narrower, with lower flux and a longer longitudinal coherence length for wide-angle measurements. Like the mirrors, reflection is horizontal to reduce sensitivity to angular vibration. Crystal pitch must stay within 40 nanoradians rms, or root-mean-square. At 30 keV and 30 m, a sideways-deflecting pair tolerates about 100 nrad of vibration before the effective source broadens by 10%, an upward-deflecting one only about 28 nrad. For pink-beam work the crystals move out of the way.

specs.vibration spec: ≤40 nrad rms pitch in the PDR
specs.Bragg range (PDR): 0° for pink-beam passage; ≈4–29° for crystal reflection
specs.vibration tolerance, 30 keV at 30 m: ≈100 nrad horizontal DCM; ≈28 nrad vertical DCM, for 10% source broadening

components.name: Mode-switch mask, 8ID-PM-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The movable mask has different settings for broad-energy pink beam and narrow-energy monochromatic beam. The monochromatic path is displaced laterally by 10 to 15 mm from the pink path, depending on the source document. The mask opening is moved to the active path.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter, 8ID-SH-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The safety shutter blocks radiation before people enter downstream enclosures, while upstream optics remain in operation. It is built to stop both pink and monochromatic beams.

components.name: Secondary collimator, 8ID-SC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The final shielding block is at the downstream wall of the first optics enclosure. It keeps scattered radiation from following the beam pipe out onto the experiment floor.

components.name: Shielded transport, 8ID-ST-1, -ST-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33: 36.0–47.0 m. The displayed position is the range start.
components.text: The beam travels through an 11 m lead-shielded vacuum pipe past 8-BM-B to the second optics enclosure. The path from source to experiment stations has no windows and remains under ultra-high vacuum, reducing wavefront distortion.

components.name: Pink-beam diagnostics, 8ID-BD-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Beam position is measured at the entrance to the second optics enclosure. In the preliminary design it combines a diamond beam-position monitor, a fluorescent screen and a bypass aperture, to measure beam stability after the 11 m transport.

components.name: Pink-beam slits, 8ID-SL-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The beam is trimmed by slits opening up to about 10 × 10 mm² before the planned multilayer monochromator. They limit stray beam and heat on the optics that follow.

components.name: Double multilayer monochromator, 8ID-MN-3/4/5, status unconfirmed
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight. Not mentioned in the 2021 status talk or the 2026 directory, which lists only Si(111)/Si(311). Installation is unconfirmed. Drawn see-through because its installation is unconfirmed.
components.text: The planned double-multilayer monochromator has two mirrors coated with alternating nanometre-scale layers. These reflect an energy band about 0.3 to 1% wide, broader than the silicon crystals, with higher transmitted flux. It was designed for small-angle speckle work, which does not need the crystals' fine energy resolution, and must move fully out of the beam otherwise. Recent descriptions of the beamline do not mention it, so it may never have been installed; it is drawn see-through.

components.name: Mode-switch mask, 8ID-PM-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: A second mode-switch mask is installed after the planned multilayer monochromator position. Like the first, it is set to match whichever beam, pink or monochromatic, is in use.

components.name: Pink-beam slits before CRL-1, 8ID-SL-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The slit opening sets the beam area entering the first lenses and the number of transverse coherent modes accepted. A smaller opening accepts fewer modes, increasing speckle contrast while reducing flux. For a single mode at 10 keV the preliminary design specifies a width × height of about 79 × 199 µm. The smaller vertical source gives a larger vertical coherent region. The design cases also use about 3.2 × 3.2 ≈ 10 modes, trading contrast for flux.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-1, Be compound refractive lenses; 8ID-TR-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Both stations share a transfocator with 12 movable stacks of curved beryllium compound refractive lenses. Refraction is weak in each lens, so many are stacked for a useful focal length. The thin-lens relation is f = R/(2Nδ), where R is apex radius, N is lens count and δ is the refractive decrement below 1. For beryllium, δ is about 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ at 10 keV and seven times smaller at 25 keV, requiring more lenses at higher energy. Zoom focusing combines this stack with the Kirkpatrick–Baez mirrors for 8-ID-E or with CRL-2 for 8-ID-I. The stack is water-cooled for pink-beam heat load and is moved laterally for alignment with the pink or monochromatic path.

specs.2D lens set (FDR): R = 1,000, 500, 300, 200 and 100 µm, 1 lens each; then stacks of 2, 4, 8 and 8 lenses at R = 100 µm
specs.1D lens set (FDR): R = 1,000 µm stacks of 1, 2 and 4 lenses

components.name: Beam-position diagnostics, 8ID-BD-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Beam position is measured just after the lenses. Monitor feedback stabilizes the beam position at the 8-ID-E sample with either pink or monochromatic beam.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter for 8-ID-E, 8ID-SH-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The safety shutter is at the downstream end of the second optics enclosure, before 8-ID-E. It blocks pink beam during 8-ID-E experiments, which use only monochromatic beam.

components.name: 8-ID-E optics table, attenuators, experiment shutter, mono-beam slits 8ID-SL-5
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 places SL-5 at 54.8 m. Attenuators and shutter share a motorized six-degree-of-freedom table, PDR TC1 at 52.5 to 54.5 m in the 2017 layout. Their positions are approximate.
components.text: A motorized table provides six-axis position adjustment for attenuating filters, a fast shutter and slits before the final focusing mirrors. The table optics are used only with monochromatic beam. Only the slit position is tabulated, at 54.8 m. Other positions are approximate.

components.name: KB focusing mirrors, bendable Kirkpatrick–Baez pair, 8ID-MR-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight. The FDR text instead places VKB/HKB 500/350 mm before the 56.3 to 56.5 m sample, conflicting with the table. The PDR gives a 0.4 m optic-to-sample distance. VKB reflects vertically before HKB reflects horizontally, both at 2.5 mrad.
components.text: In the Kirkpatrick–Baez arrangement, the first curved mirror focuses vertically and the second horizontally. With CRL-1, the focus reaches about 0.3 µm. Speckle size is approximately wavelength × distance ÷ spot size. A small focus therefore produces speckles large enough to resolve at a practical distance. The platinum-coated mirrors meet the beam at 2.5 mrad and are bent to shape; their surfaces must match the ideal shape to within 1.0 to 1.5 nm rms, or root-mean-square. Unlike lenses, mirrors focus every energy to the same point. The first mirror is the only optic on 8-ID that deflects the beam vertically.

specs.benders: Bimorph benders specified in the PDR
specs.figure tolerance: 1.5 nm horizontal and 1.0 nm vertical rms
specs.deflections: VKB upstream, vertical; HKB downstream, horizontal. The upward or downward VKB deflection is undocumented.

components.name: Be window, 8ID-WN-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: A thin beryllium window separates the optics vacuum from the sample area. It is chosen to preserve the beam's coherence.

components.name: Guard slits, 8ID-SL-6
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The final slits are just before the sample. They block the faint halo scattered by upstream optics, and the fringes diffracted by the edges of earlier slits, so that they do not obscure the sample's weak speckle.

components.name: Six-circle diffractometer, Huber design, with sample stack; 8ID-BI-1, -BI-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight. Other FDR passages quote 56.4/56.5 m for the wide-angle sample.
components.text: A stiff six-circle diffractometer sets sample orientation for measurements at selected crystal reflections. Its split detector arm carries a close detector that swings upward and a rail that supports the long flight path to the far detector. The undulator light is horizontally polarized. In the horizontal scattering plane, intensity falls as cos²(2θ) at large scattering angle 2θ. Vertical-plane scattering avoids this polarization suppression. Its base slides aside to let the beam through to 8-ID-I.

components.name: 8-ID-E sample environments
components.distanceNote: At the diffractometer centre.
components.text: Interchangeable sample stages support heating, cooling and tensile loading. A liquid-helium cryostage covers 3.5 K to 475 K, a vacuum dome reaches 1,100 °C, and a tensile stage operates from liquid-nitrogen temperature to 350 °C. The lowest cryostage temperature is 3.5 degrees above absolute zero. The 2021 plan also listed a second heating and cooling stage covering 93 to 773 K.

specs.models: Lake Shore ST-500; Anton Paar DHS 1100; Linkam MFS

components.name: Removable beam-pass pipe, 8ID-VP-2; for 8-ID-I and USAXS modes
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33: 57.3–61.0 m. The displayed position is the range start. Drawn see-through, as the model shows 8-ID-E in WA mode.
components.text: A removable vacuum pipe spans 8-ID-E during 8-ID-I operation. The two experiment stations take turns: when 8-ID-I is in use, the diffractometer slides aside and this 3.7 m pipe carries the beam straight through 8-ID-E. Its windows must survive pink beam, so they are water-cooled and purged with nitrogen. It is drawn see-through because this model shows 8-ID-E in wide-angle mode.

components.name: Vertical-arm WA detector, 1.5–2 m, on the diffractometer arm
components.distanceNote: MEDSI 2020 gives an approximate sample distance of 1.5 to 2 m. The FDR lists flight path 8ID-BI-2 at 58.0 m. The model detector is at 1.6 m and 2θ = 30° upward, 57.7 m along the beam and 0.8 m above it. This is illustrative, like the LDDP setting.
components.text: The near detector is mounted on the diffractometer arm, 1.5 to 2 m from the sample. Its upward movement reaches scattering angles up to 120° in the design for atomic-scale speckle measurements. Being close, it spreads each speckle over fewer pixels than the far detector does, but scattering upward avoids the polarization loss at large angles. A short flight pipe, anti-scatter slits and a remote filter box sit between it and the sample.

components.name: Long-distance detector positioner, LDDP, with air-bearing base and removable flight path
components.distanceNote: The FDR lists 8ID-DT-1 at 60.0 m, about 3.7 m from the sample. The LDDP range is 2.5 to 4 m. The model uses R = 3.7 m and 2θ = 30° outboard, at 59.5 m along the beam and 1.85 m outboard. This illustrates a metallic-glass peak at q about 2.6 Å⁻¹ and about 10 keV.
components.text: The detector positioner rests on air cushions over granite for positioning at 2.5 to 4 m from the sample and horizontal angles of 3 to 55°. Farther away, each speckle spreads over more pixels and is easier to resolve. Removable vacuum flight-path sections bridge the gap from the diffractometer, motorized stages fine-tune the position, and a laser tracker records exactly where the detector ended up.

components.name: Diagnostics for 8-ID-I, 8ID-BD-5
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Beam position is measured for orbit corrections at the 8-ID-I station. In the design it combines a diamond position monitor, a fluorescent screen and a bypass aperture, and its feedback corrects slow drifts of the monochromator and mirrors.

components.name: Pink-beam slits before CRL-2, 8ID-SL-7
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Slits define the coherent part of the beam entering CRL-2. As with the slits before CRL-1, the opening trades coherence against photon count; they open up to 10 × 10 mm² and are rated for pink beam.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-2, 8ID-TR-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: A second movable beryllium-lens stack is installed about five metres before the small-angle sample, with the same lens set as CRL-1. Working together, the two transfocators set the spot at the 8-ID-I sample between about 3 and 10 µm; simulations at 14.2 keV, with about ten coherent modes accepted, give 3.0 × 2.0 µm at the smallest and 11 × 8.5 µm at the largest. The whole unit travels ±300 mm along the beam to keep the focus on the sample across 8–25 keV.

components.name: Pink-beam shutter for 8-ID-I, 8ID-SH-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The safety shutter is upstream of the small-angle station, 8-ID-I. It blocks either pink or monochromatic radiation before people enter 8-ID-I, while upstream delivery continues.

components.name: Through-wall shielded pipe, 8ID-ST-3, 8-ID-E/8-ID-I wall
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The beam travels through a short shielded pipe in the wall between the experiment stations. The pipe is rated for pink-beam operation at 8-ID-I.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #1, 8ID-SL-8
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The first of three precision slit stages on the upstream 8-ID-I table removes radiation near the beam edges. Each stage trims the faint tails left by the one before. Between the slits and the sample the vacuum is held by differential pumping. Separately pumped sections reduce pressure in stages without a window.

components.name: Fast shutter and attenuators, 8-ID-I
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate, on the upstream optical table at about 64 to 66.5 m. The FDR table does not list it.
components.text: A sub-millisecond shutter and polished attenuating filters control exposure across 8 to 25 keV. They sit on the upstream optical table; the position shown is approximate.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #2, 8ID-SL-9
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The second precision slit stage removes faint scatter from the edges of the first stage.

components.name: 8-ID-I guard slits #3, 8ID-SL-10
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The final guard slit is placed just before the sample. Set just outside the beam, it blocks scatter from the slits upstream without clipping the beam itself.

components.name: Be window, 8ID-WN-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin beryllium window just before the sample. Beryllium, a very light metal, transmits X-rays with little absorption while holding the vacuum.

components.name: 8-ID-I sample table and environments, including Rheo-XPCS, 8ID-BI-4 and -BI-6
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight. The 2021 drawing puts the table at about 66.1 m; uncertainty is ±1 m.
components.text: Small-angle samples are mounted on this table. The interchangeable mounts include a heated holder for up to nine samples at three temperatures between 0 and 160 °C. A rheometer holds fluid between two cylinders in a Couette cell for simultaneous shear and XPCS measurements. The beam crosses the cell centre along the direction in which the flow speed changes, so the speckle records motion along the flow and along the cylinder axis.

specs.rheometer: Anton Paar MCR 702e with twin drive and Couette cell

components.name: 12 m SAXS flight tube, telescoping 4–12 m, rotatable 5°; 8ID-BI-5
components.distanceNote: The FDR places the tube start at 68.0 m and detector at 79.0 m. A 2025 as-built abstract gives a 4 to 12 m sample-to-detector distance and 5° horizontal rotation. The model shows full extension from 68.0 to 78.85 m, with the selection pin at mid-length, 73 m.
components.text: Scattered X-rays travel through a vacuum tube up to 12 m long. Speckle size increases with detector distance, making the pattern easier to resolve on individual pixels. The tube telescopes from 4 to 12 m and swings up to 5° about the sample to reach larger angles, and its far end carries a motorized beam stop and a Kapton window. When stationary, the detector end must hold still to within 200 nm. In one published run at 12.4 keV with the detector at 11.6 m, it covered scattering vectors q from 0.04 to 0.51 nm⁻¹.

components.name: Fast photon-counting detectors, Rigaku Si 3-Mpixel PAD and Dectris EIGER2 X CdTe 4M; 8ID-DT-2
components.distanceNote: The FDR detector position is 79.0 m at the 12 m flight-path end. It moves with the telescoping tube. The model uses the FDR position, 11.5 m from the FDR sample.
components.text: Incident photons are counted in each pixel of the small-angle detectors. The Rigaku silicon 3-megapixel detector records up to 56,000 frames a second continuously with 19.2 µs time resolution and close to a million a second in short bursts; at full speed it produces about 164 GB of raw data a second. The DECTRIS EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, whose cadmium-telluride sensor stops high-energy X-rays efficiently, runs at up to 4 kHz. The displayed detector pattern is simulated. Outer speckles change faster because they correspond to smaller spatial scales.

specs.fast PAD: Rigaku Si 3 MPix, "UHSS 3M", 56 kHz continuous. The XSPA-500k characterization uses 2-bit readout. The XSPA family has 13-frame bursts up to about 1 MHz.
specs.high-energy PAD: EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, up to 4 kHz in the directory

components.name: Beam stop, 8ID-BS-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.33 records distance from the centre of the insertion-device straight.
components.text: Remaining pink or monochromatic radiation is absorbed by a beam stop at 80.6 m. During measurements a small motorized stop inside the flight tube absorbs the direct beam, so it never hits the detector.

enclosures.name: Storage-ring tunnel / front end
enclosures.notes: The straight centre is the origin for the undulators. The 2021 elevation places the HHLFE at about 14–25 m and the ratchet-wall exit at about 24.5 m.

enclosures.name: 8-ID-A
enclosures.role: Existing first optics enclosure, reused for the upgrade
enclosures.notes: The PDR gives 24–36 m. This enclosure contains the front-end exit table, white-beam slits, M1/M2, stops, collimators, HDCM, mode-switch mask and SH-1. The width is approximate, from the 2021 plan. The enclosure extends about 1.3 m outboard of the beam and 0.6–1 m toward the ratchet wall, which it adjoins on its inboard side.

enclosures.name: Shielded transport
enclosures.role: Lead-shielded vacuum transport on the experiment floor
enclosures.notes: FDR transport sections 8ID-ST-1/2 extend from 36.0–47.0 m, beside the outboard side of hutch 8-BM-B.

enclosures.name: 8-ID-D
enclosures.role: New second optics enclosure for pink and monochromatic beam
enclosures.notes: The boundaries are from the 2021 plan with about ±0.2 m uncertainty. The PDR envelope is 7 m long × 2 m wide × 3 m high. Components are BD-3, SL-3, the optional DMM, PM-4, SL-4, CRL-1, BD-4 and SH-2. The elevation gives a roof height of about 3.4 m.

enclosures.name: 8-ID-E
enclosures.role: New wide-angle XPCS experimental hutch, also used for beam passage and the USAXS sample
enclosures.notes: The 2021 plan places the outboard inner wall about 4.05 m from the beam along 53.9–61.8 m, stepping inward to about 1.8 m along 61.8–63.7 m. The opposite wall slopes from about 1.3 m to 2.2 m from the beam. The roof is about 4.2 m high, compared with 3.4 m elsewhere, to clear the vertical detector arm. Stairs are at the upstream outboard corner. The diffractometer is at about 56.3 m. The 55° LDDP arc extends outboard. CRL-2 and SH-3 at the downstream end are used for 8-ID-I.

enclosures.name: 8-ID control room
enclosures.role: New control room for both stations, outside the radiation shielding
enclosures.notes: The 2021 plan shows a wedge-shaped room outboard of 8-ID-E and 8-ID-I. The PDR specifies a temperature-controlled room encompassing the hutch entrances. The plan places the upstream wall at about 54.1 m. The outer wall runs diagonally from about 8.8 m outboard at 56.7 m to the 8-ID-I wall at 75.5 m. Desks are along the outer wall, with doors near 70–74 m.

enclosures.name: 8-ID-I
enclosures.role: New small-angle XPCS and Rheo-XPCS experimental hutch, also used for the USAXS detector. It extends beyond the standard experimental aisle.
enclosures.notes: The 2021 plan places the walls about 1.9 m outboard and 2.2–2.8 m inboard of the beam, giving a maximum width of about 4.7 m. The downstream end tapers to a point at about 81.6 m. The 12 m flight tube occupies about 67–79 m; its 5° rotation extends toward the inboard 9-BM side. The extension beyond the experimental aisle was approved in record of decision APSU_2040668, cited in the 2021 talk.

instruments.name: WA-XPCS instrument, six-circle diffractometer and LDDP
instruments.text: At the wide-angle station, the sample and detector rotate about six axes on a stable six-circle diffractometer. A beryllium CRL-1 stack and Kirkpatrick–Baez mirror pair focus the beam to 0.3–3 µm. The detector is positioned on an upward-rotating arm 1.5–2 m away or on the long-distance positioner up to 4 m away, at horizontal angles of 3–55°. At the longer distance, atomic-scale speckle covers more pixels. Sample-to-detector geometry is measured with a laser tracker. Removable vacuum paths and anti-scatter slits reduce air scatter. Configurations include short-distance vertical scattering, long-distance horizontal scattering and pinhole ultra-small-angle scattering with the detector in 8-ID-I. For 8-ID-I operation, the diffractometer is moved aside.
detectors: Rigaku Si 3 MPix fast pixel-array detector, 56 kHz and burst ≈1 MHz
Dectris EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, up to 4 kHz in the directory
sampleEnvironments: Lake Shore ST-500 liquid-helium cryostage, 3.5–475 K
Anton Paar DHS 1100 vacuum heating dome, ≤1,100 °C
Linkam MFS tensile stage, from liquid-nitrogen temperature to 350 °C
Anton Paar DCS-500, 93–773 K in the 2021 plan

instruments.name: SA-XPCS instrument, sample table and 4–12 m flight tube
instruments.text: At the small-angle station, scattered X-rays pass through a telescoping vacuum tube 4–12 m long before reaching a photon-counting detector. Speckle size at the detector increases with this distance. Beryllium lens stacks CRL-1 and CRL-2 produce a 3–10 µm spot with pink or monochromatic beam. An upstream table supports three precision guard slits, a fast shutter, attenuators and beryllium windows. Heated cells or a rheometer are installed on the sample table. The tube rotates up to 5° about the sample for larger scattering angles. Its downstream end has a motorized beam stop and Kapton window.
sampleEnvironments: Holder with 9 samples in 3 temperature zones, 0–160 °C
Anton Paar MCR 702e rheometer for Rheo-XPCS
In-vacuum polymer-melt stage, −20 to 225 °C in the 2021 plan

instruments.name: Rheo-SAXS-XPCS with the Center for Nanoscale Materials
instruments.text: At the Rheo-XPCS station, fluid is sheared steadily or oscillated in the gap between two cylinders. This measurement is offered with Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials. The Anton Paar MCR 702e has two independent drives and a Couette cell. X-rays cross the cell centre along the velocity-gradient direction, with motion measured along the flow and cylinder axis. Steady or oscillatory shear, creep and recovery tests run during speckle acquisition at 10 to 100,000 frames per second. Stress and strain are then compared with particle motion.
detectors: EIGER2 X CdTe 4M, for example at 11.6 m

instruments.name: Pinhole USAXS and US-XPCS configuration
instruments.text: The sample is placed on the 8-ID-E diffractometer and the detector at the end of the 8-ID-I flight tube, about 22 m away. This distance resolves very small scattering angles from structures up to micrometres in size and their slow motion. The beam size is 15–45 µm. Wide-angle scattering in 8-ID-E is recorded simultaneously when its detector is in use.

geometryNotes:
The beam follows one axis without canting. All enclosures are on the main experiment floor in sector 8, with no extension to the Long Beamline Building.

The reused 8-ID-A first optics enclosure spans about 24.6 to 36.0 m. An approximately 11 m shielded transport at 36 to 47 m passes 8-BM-B. The narrow 8-ID-D second optics enclosure spans about 46.8 to 53.9 m and is about 2 m wide. E spans 53.9 to 63.7 m and has the tallest roof, about 4.2 m. I spans 63.7 to 81.6 m in a tapering wedge extending beyond the standard hutch aisle. A wedge-shaped control room is outboard of E/I; 9-BM is inboard.

All upstream transport optics reflect horizontally, including M1/M2, HDCM and the FDR multilayer monochromator. Only the vertical KB mirror at E reflects vertically, at 2.5 mrad grazing angle and about 5 mrad beam deflection. Its upward or downward direction is undocumented.

interactiveIdeas.title: Brownian motion and speckle correlations
interactiveIdeas.concept: Particles undergo Brownian motion in water or glycerol. Controls change particle size, temperature and viscosity. A simulated detector displays far-field speckle |sum_j exp(i q.r_j)|² for a Gaussian illumination footprint. Selecting a ring of pixels calculates g2(τ). A fit returns the diffusion coefficient and particle size through the Stokes–Einstein relation.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Speckle depends on particle positions, and its fluctuation rate measures motion. Correlations decay faster at larger q. Viscosity and particle size determine the Brownian time scale.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: For Brownian motion, the Siegert relation gives g2 = 1 + β exp(−2 D q² τ). Intensity correlations decay at twice the field rate. Diffusion follows D = kT/(6 π η R). Silica particles of radius R = 57 nm in water at 25 °C have D ≈4.3 × 10⁻¹² m²/s. At q = 0.05 nm⁻¹, 1/(Dq²) ≈93 µs and the g2 decay time is about 46 µs, requiring microsecond detection. Glycerol produces diffusion about 1,000× slower. Scattering vector q = 4 π sin(θ)/λ, with λ[Å] = 12.398/E[keV]. Partial coherence and pixel averaging reduce contrast to β <1. Pixel counts include Poisson photon noise.

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherent flux and time resolution
interactiveIdeas.concept: Controls select a relaxation time from 1 ms to 1 µs and the 2019 APS or APS-U source. Simulated frames include the photon budget, with mostly zero counts and occasional single photons. The calculated g2 curve includes photon noise and a signal-to-noise estimate. Increasing frame rate reduces counts per frame, with the higher coherent flux allowing faster decays to remain measurable.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: XPCS time resolution depends on coherent flux and photon statistics. Under fixed acquisition conditions, time resolution scales with the square of coherent intensity. Fast low-bit-depth readout is useful when most pixels receive very few photons per frame.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: In the low-count regime I_pix dt <<1, SNR(g2) ≈β * I_pix * sqrt(T * dt * N_pix). Pixel intensity I_pix is proportional to coherent flux Fc, scattering cross-section and pixel solid angle. Fc = B λ²/4. The pre-upgrade 8-ID-I benchmark was about 2 × 10¹⁰ ph/s coherent at 7.4 keV in 2016. The design value is about 10¹³ ph/s with Si(111) near 10 keV in one mode. At fixed SNR, dt_min scales as Fc⁻². The microsecond-frame simulation retains low photon counts, typically no more than a few per pixel per frame.

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom focusing and detector sampling
interactiveIdeas.concept: Controls select beryllium CRL cartridges with R = 100–1,000 µm in CRL-1 and CRL-2, or change KB curvature, at 8–25 keV. The displayed sample spot ranges from 0.3–3 µm in 8-ID-E and 3–10 µm in 8-ID-I. A second view compares detector speckle size with 75 µm pixels at distances of 1.5–12 m. Measured contrast decreases when speckles are smaller than pixels.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Speckle size grows with detector distance and falls with illuminated sample size. Higher energies reduce speckle size and weaken refraction. Focal spot, accepted coherent modes and transmitted flux must be considered together.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: For a thin CRL, f = R/(2 N δ). For Be, δ ≈3.4 × 10⁻⁶ at 10 keV and scales as 1/E², giving about 5.4 × 10⁻⁷ at 25 keV. With N = 10 and R = 100 µm, f is about 1.5 m at 10 keV and 9 m at 25 keV. Speckle size s = λ R / a. At 10 keV with R = 12 m, a = 3 µm gives about 0.5 mm speckles and a = 10 µm gives about 150 µm. At 25 keV with a = 10 µm and R = 12 m, the result is about 60 µm, smaller than a pixel. At the WA station, 10 keV with a = 0.3 µm and R = 1.5 m gives about 0.6 mm. KB focusing is achromatic, while CRL focusing is chromatic. The far-field condition is R >a²/λ.

interactiveIdeas.title: Aging and two-time correlation maps
interactiveIdeas.concept: An animated speckle sequence for an aging colloidal gel or metallic glass at 668 K is used to calculate a growing two-time map C(t1,t2). Controls change the aging exponent and add intermittent rearrangements. The diagonal band widens as relaxation slows, and abrupt events produce blocks of correlations.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Dynamics in a material out of equilibrium change with sample age. A single averaged g2 curve obscures this variation. Two-time maps distinguish aging and intermittent rearrangements, as in the 83-hour metallic-glass measurement.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Over pixels at fixed q, C(t1,t2) = <I(t1)I(t2)>/(<I(t1)><I(t2)>). The diagonal width scales approximately as τ(t_age) ∝t_age^µ. The KWW form is f = exp[−(t/τ)^β_KWW]. Compressed exponents β_KWW ≈1.2–2 are typical of stress-driven glass dynamics. A stationary regime has constant diagonal width.

interactiveIdeas.title: Rheo-XPCS and flow-direction correlations
interactiveIdeas.concept: A Couette cell has fluid between two cylinders, with controls for stress and shear rate. Dense-suspension rheology is plotted with viscosity, stress and g2. Flow-direction g2 decays faster under shear and shows oscillations when a jammed network coexists with mobile particles. The corresponding vorticity-direction correlations do not show these flow oscillations.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Rheology measures bulk thickening, yielding and memory, while XPCS measures particle motion. Correlations depend on direction. Heterodyne oscillations arise from relative motion between scattering populations.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: The beam follows the velocity-gradient direction, with q in the flow-vorticity plane. Uniform shear across the illuminated gap adds flow-direction decorrelation proportional to sinc²(q_par * γ̇ * w * τ / 2), where w is the path through the sheared region. Two populations with relative velocity v produce cos(q.v τ) oscillations in g2. Vorticity-direction g2 measures only non-affine, diffusive motion.

interactiveIdeas.title: Polarization and scattering-plane intensity
interactiveIdeas.concept: Field vectors indicate horizontal polarization of the undulator beam. Controls rotate a detector in the horizontal or vertical plane around the sample and plot intensity against 2θ.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: For horizontally polarized X-rays, scattering intensity in the horizontal plane vanishes near 90°. The horizontal long-distance arm resolves finer speckle at smaller angles, while the vertical arm covers large angles without this polarization suppression.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: The Thomson polarization factor is approximately cos²(2θ) for horizontal-plane scattering and 1 for vertical-plane scattering. At the LDDP limit of 2θ = 55°, cos²(55°) = 0.33. The horizontal factor is zero at 90°. The PDR vertical-arm range reaches 120°. At 2θ = 55°, q = 4.7 Å⁻¹ at 10 keV and 11.7 Å⁻¹ at 25 keV.

interactiveIdeas.title: Transverse and longitudinal coherence
interactiveIdeas.concept: Controls select slit opening, monochromator and sample thickness, with pink beam at about 0.5% bandwidth or Si(111)/Si(311). A scattering-angle control changes the calculated path difference. Displayed speckle contrast decreases when path differences exceed longitudinal coherence length or slit opening exceeds transverse coherence length.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Transverse coherence depends on source size, while longitudinal coherence depends on bandwidth. Small-angle measurements tolerate broader bandwidth. Pink beam has about 100× higher photon flux, but wide-angle measurements require narrower bandwidth to maintain contrast.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: With ξL ≈λ²/Δλ, longitudinal coherence at 10 keV is about 0.95 µm for Si(111), 4.6 µm for Si(311) and 25 nm for 0.5% pink beam. In transmission, path-length difference PLD ≈2 t sin²(θ) + w sin(2θ), where t is sample thickness and w is illuminated width in the scattering plane. Contrast persists when PLD is less than roughly ξL. This uses the PDR convention ξL = λ²/Δλ; some texts use λ²/(2 Δλ), half as large. Transverse coherence is about λ L/(2 π Σ). At 52 m and 10 keV, the APS-U values are about 70 µm horizontally and 250 µm vertically.

funFacts: 8-ID was the first APS Upgrade feature beamline to host users, with a University of Akron group in November 2024.
Sutton, Mochrie and colleagues first observed X-ray speckle in 1991, as reported in Nature. Grübel, Mochrie and Sutton received the APS Compton Award in 2009 for their work on the technique.

When photon statistics set the limit, 100× higher coherent flux permits 10,000× shorter XPCS frames at fixed measurement quality, acquisition time, speckle contrast and pixel count. Detector speed and sample dose also limit the improvement.
Each revolver undulator has two magnet arrays with 21 and 25 mm periods mounted at 90° on one rotating support. Rotation places the selected array around the electron beam.
A Rigaku 3-Mpixel detector at 56,000 frames per second produces about 164 GB/s of raw data. Expected annual beamline volume is up to about 20 PB, about 200× the pre-upgrade volume.
A wide-angle XPCS measurement of metallic glass at 8-ID-E lasted 83 hours, or 300,000 s, with one frame every 2.5 s. The data showed intermittent atomic rearrangements.
The specified monochromator vibration tolerance is less than 40 nanoradians.

Before the upgrade, 8-ID-E and 8-ID-I were among the longest and tallest APS enclosures. More than 3,000 experiments were conducted there over 25 years. In 2022, six workers emptied both enclosures in under 14 days, as reported on 3 October 2022.
The 8-ID-I design includes a 12 m flight tube and a 22 m USAXS configuration. Its extension beyond the standard experiment-floor aisle required formal approval.
Before the upgrade, diffusion of Cowpea mosaic virus in solution was measured at 8-ID-I with 19 µs resolution. XPCS measurements on a freely suspended robotic pendant drop reached 3.7 µs resolution.

openQuestions: The optional double-multilayer monochromator at 49 m is listed as 8ID-MN-3/4/5 in the FDR. Neither the 2021 status talk nor the 2026 directory mentions it; the directory lists only Si(111)/Si(311). It may have been removed from scope or deferred.
FDR 2019 Table 4.33 and the 2021 drawing differ by up to about 1 m in 8-ID-I. The sample is at 67.5 m in the table and about 66.1 m in the drawing. No installed-component position table is public.
The HDCM lateral offset is 15 mm in FDR Fig. 4.23 and about 10 mm in the PDR and 2021 talk. Its inboard or outboard direction is undocumented.

The FDR table places the KB at 55.3 m. The text places the VKB and HKB 500 and 350 mm upstream of a sample at 56.3–56.5 m, which would put them after the Be window at 55.7 m. The exhibit uses the table order.
The FDR text describes M2 as flat with an optional bender, but its component table labels it "Focusing". Installation of a bender is unconfirmed.
The 2025 flight-path abstract gives a 4–12 m range for 8-ID-I. The 2021 requirement gives 2–12 m.

Energy ranges differ between sources. The FDR gives 8–25 keV, the 2021 WA table gives 4.8–25 keV, and the 2026 directory gives 6–25 or 7–25 keV. The practical low-energy limit with U25 and the HDCM is undocumented. At the 8.5 mm device minimum gap, the U25 fundamental has E1 ≥4.5 keV.

The Rigaku "Si 3 MPix" public model name is unspecified; the computing strategy calls it "UHSS 3M". The directory Eiger CdTe 4M rate of 4 kHz matches the APS planning table of 4.0 MB frames at 4 kHz, or 1 byte/pixel. Reduced-bit-depth operation is inferred, but not confirmed by DECTRIS specifications.

As of 8 October 2026, the source review found no peer-reviewed commissioning paper with measured APS-U coherent flux, speckle contrast or stability at 8-ID. The quoted flux values are design or directory values.
The 8-ID page dates general-user operations to October 2024. News reports date the first users to early November 2024.
The control-room side, LDDP arc direction and flight-tube rotation side are inferred from the 2021 plan, rather than explicitly stated as inboard or outboard.
The revolver centre positions and phase-shifter details in the straight are approximate.

The 2021 WA-XPCS table gives 1–2 × 10¹² ph/s for one mode with Si(111) over 8–25 keV. This is about 10× below FDR/PDR design values of 1.6–1.7 × 10¹³ at 8.8–10 keV. The reason is undocumented, and no measured installed value is public.
The upward or downward VKB deflection and resulting WA sample height relative to the beam axis are undocumented.
